utterances.text: When it was in Dobrinja, can you tell us, if you know, where it was stationed in Dobrinja when it was there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Most of the time, in one of those facilities in the immediate vicinity of the command post because I repeat, it was under the direct command of the commander of this brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, as far as I have understood you from your markings, you have marked on this map command posts of brigades. Did I understand you correctly, except that in two places, you have marked a forward command post, and here you have marked a command post of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I was led by the principle that in this way, we can show the objectives of -- the targets of operative importance. These were the combat dispositions that had its positions in different facilities which were not military facilities. For instance, kindergarten or primary school buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have information at that time as to where the command posts or battalions were and of other smaller units that were in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But I told you in the beginning that I have forgotten things, and I couldn't be absolutely precise in listing them. These that I have marked are certainly those that are the most important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have information within brigades how many battalions there were and lower units, smaller units, in the area of responsibility of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: BH army was reorganised several times. And this was one of the latest establishments of the army. The 1st Corps was reorganised into three divisions. The corps commander was Brigadier Nedzad Ajhadzic. The 12th division was located in Sarajevo, and the commander was Fikret Prevljak. The 14th division was located in Tarcin, and the 16th division was located in Vares. This corps had as far as we knew about 30.300 soldiers. And they were distributed in eight brigades that we showed on this map. And five independent units ranging from regiment to brigade. As far as the organisation was concerned, it was a tripartite organisation, and using some structure from the former JNA. That is, the brigade had three infantry battalions, and the usual units attached to the staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, in the period 1992, 1993, did you know whether the area of responsibility in the 1st Corps in the part of the city under their control, were there any other units that were not subordinate to the corps, but were active in that area? Did you have such information?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I said at the beginning that in the city itself, there were about 38.000 armed troops. Out of that, there were 30.300, or let's say 31.000, were in the BH army units, were part of BH army units. And several special units, special MUP units also existed in Sarajevo, in the part of Sarajevo under Muslim control. And we assessed that these troops amounted to the strength of one brigade. And they were made up of special units like the special detachment Laste or swallows. Then another unit called Biseri, that is, pearls, and some others I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, before the break, you told us about the forward command post in Lukavica. Can you tell us, in the period relevant for the Defence, do you have any information whether there were other forward command posts in certain locations during this period? And if there were any --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, depending on the situation on the front, the commander would side and would, therefore, order the establishment of a forward command post at a given location, at a given part of the front. If there is a need for that, if the situation made it necessary in order to conduct the operations and -- of command and also in order to follow the situation more easily. And so we did have those needs, and occasionally, we would establish a forward command post in Trnovo, in Butile, Vogosca, Nisic plateau or Nisic Visoravan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that these forward command posts were established depending on the need, and then those forward command posts, the corps commander would be, can you tell us, when you say that the situation would make it necessary for this to happen, can you tell us how long would then a commander have to be there? According to your recollection, at those command posts, for how long would a commander need to be at one of those locations? I know that you said this would depend on the situation, but I was wondering if you could tell us how long that would be, would that be one month, two months, or one day, two days?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The establishment of the forward command post would be decided on by the commander for the reasons that I have already explained. And most of the time, this occurred because there would be an attack of Muslims units on a certain part of the front. This forward command post, therefore, existed as long as it was necessary. And most of the time, that would be 10 to 15 days until the situation on the front would stabilise. In some areas, that would last longer. For instance, at Nisic plateau or in Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say at certain locations longer, at Nisic plateau and Trnovo, can you tell us what period this was, between September 1992 and August 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, that would be in 1993, from July -- say from about August until July. So approximately a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, you told us in the barracks that we saw on the videorecording, you said that you saw General Galic there, and that you attended meetings that were held at the command. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes. As a head of the intelligence section, during the absence of the chief for intelligence and security, I would go in his place, and I would take part in the work of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, how many such meetings, such official meetings, so to speak, did you attend? And we're talking about the period from when the General was there until he left.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: In percentages, that would be about 30 per cent. Attended about 30 per cent of meetings, 20 to 30 per cent of meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, at those meetings, those morning meetings, who attended?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The way that the corps command worked, the commander made it an obligation to have a morning meeting, and this was an extensive meeting. And its objective was that the organs of the command learn about the situation on the front in the previous 12 hours, of the previous night. Those organs of the command and the commander at the beginning of the meeting would be informed on the basis of written reports that arrived at the operations centre. As the meeting went on, on the basis of reports that came from subordinate units, commander made certain decisions and issued some orders, and they were in relation to the problems that the subordinate units formulated in their reports. These were mostly matters of logistics support, of MTS, materiel and technical equipment, fuel, ammunition, clothes, footwear, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point, when you were talking about the morning meetings, you said that these were extensive meetings of the command. Can you tell us whether at those meetings that you call the extensive meetings, did the chief for the -- cooperation with UNPROFOR also attend and the operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: I have just explained that the duty operations officer had a task and a duty to inform the organs of the command about the situation in the units, while the officer, the chief of the cooperation, that is liaison officer with UNPROFOR, he did not attend these meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted this clarification precisely so that I could ask a question in relation to the extensive composition of the command. Did it mean that there were other types of meetings or other meetings which did not encompass the extensive command structure?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, although these were rare meetings. But the close command, the corps command, that would be the chief of staff, that would be assistant commander for intelligence and security, and assistant commander for religion, morale, and legal matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, you told us that at those more extended meetings, the duty operations officer reported on the situation in the area of responsibility of the corps on the basis of written reports received from subordinate units. Can you tell us, what was included in those reports by subordinate units when we're talking about the situation in the certain area of responsibility of those subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: These were done according to a form, these reports. The first item, the report would be the situation in the units. That is in the area of responsibility of the units. Under that item, item 1, the subordinate command would report on enemy activity, on the operations that were undertaken, on fire, on the targets that were fired on by the enemy, and also the consequences suffered by our forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the duty operations officer informed the command also about the -- when the cease-fire -- about the violations of the cease-fires in those reports?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that would be included in the first item of the report where the subordinates would inform about the enemy fire and the enemy operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to show the witness a document that we disclosed to the Prosecution. And this is D1235. Exhibit D1235.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher, could you please assist Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to give all of these to the interpreters, although some of them have been translated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, this document has a first page which is in B/C/S. Do you have it? I can see it on the ELMO. You're looking at the B/C/S text. Can you tell us, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I said. The usual form of a daily report, regular daily report. That would be the commander of the Rajlovac Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document in the top left corner has a date.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: November the 7th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was sent to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: It was sent by the command of the Rajlovac brigade, to the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and there is also the signature of the commander of this brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please read under item 1, does it say below that that this is a regular daily report, November 7 the situation until 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please read Item 1/1.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: "At 12.30, in defence area at Spajic farm in Brijesce, 12 rifle grenades fell on to this area fired from the direction of Centrotrans and Brijesko Brdo and there weren't any serious consequences. Also during the afternoon, the enemy fired snipers, from snipers on our positions in barracks of Brijesce. There were not any consequences."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bukva, this report, is this report telling us that in the area of this brigade, that there were operations, that there was firing activity?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, operations by Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, can you tell us, in your opinion, first of all, how long did you spend in this area? When I say "how long did you spend there," I mean in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps in the period from the 6th of September until the 10th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: In general, in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, I was there almost constantly except for a brief period of time when I went to visit my family. To be precise, this meant that -- again, depending on the situation, but on average, after two months at the corps, I would go and visit my family for seven days. I did not have any other periods of leave outside of the area of responsibility of the corps on any other basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you know, how frequently were combats in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and how intense were these battles?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: There were very rare situations where there was no fighting, whether there were no operations in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Regardless of several signed cease-fires signed by both sides, most frequently cease-fire that was signed would be violated by the Muslim side. And so the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was very specific in this sense, meaning that it was engaged in combat almost incessantly, in combat to a higher or lesser degree. But operations were ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to show the witness document Exhibit Number D719.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic, I have been wondering for the last two minutes of your questions what new elements you tried to elicit from this witness, apart from the many testimonies we heard from other witnesses, that there was a frequent combat activities and that cease-fires were violated by the Muslim side is not an issue that I hear for the first time, to just say it very gently. So would you please perhaps especially concentrate on what this witness could add. Of course, I'm not saying that if there are important points where he could confirm earlier evidence that you couldn't ask him about it, but especially what he would add to your case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the report the Defence showed to the witness, the date is 7th of November, 1992. And for this date, we had testimony of witnesses -- there were witnesses who said that it was peaceful that day, that there was no firing. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last two minutes of your questions were not specific to that date. And it was not clear to me what you wanted to demonstrate. Your question, the first one of these two minutes, can you tell us how frequently were the combats in the area of responsibility of the SRK and how intense were these battles, which is a very general question. I'm not asking, seeking now clarification. The witness has answered your questions. But could you please keep in mind the level of relevance of the issues you're raising. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But I just have to clarify that the witness was speaking about a report for the previous 12 hours of the 7th of November, 1992. And this is the document dated 7th of November, 1992. So in this report, in this report, the corps command is informed that in the area, as the witness read out, that there were combat operations and that there was firing as it says in the report from snipers, from sniper weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic, I do not want to enter into a debate, one of your questions was about a period of September to August and not specific. When I am referring to the two minutes, I'm referring to general information and not on your specific questions on the report, which I do understand that you want to elicit information from that. But the last two minutes were rather general and not specific for that period. Let's not spend any more time on it. I asked you to keep that in mind, and I am convinced that you will try to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have report number 720 dated the 25th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Of the 25th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. 25th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I'm sorry, but it is 719.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, is the date of this report the 25th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read out item 1 of this report.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: It's a report that the SRK command sends. It's a regular report that it sends to the main staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects to the use of these documents. There is a general objection in respect to the authenticity of these documents that the Defence has not established. And there's a specific objection as to -- that the Defence has not laid a foundation of the witness's knowledge as to the facts of the contents of these documents, testifying to the contents of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first question is to the authenticity. I know that the matter has been raised by the Prosecution. Until now, the Chamber usually has allowed questions in respect of these documents. But the second part, specific knowledge of the witness in respect of these documents, could you please try to find the basis for that, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, before I showed these documents to you, you told us that you attended morning meetings and that the duty officer reported on the situation with regard to 12-hour period to the command at these morning meetings. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, that was one way I had of becoming familiar with the contents of these reports. But in addition, as the chief of the intelligence department, I also participated to a certain extent in providing elements that were used for compiling such reports. So I was certainly in a position to be aware, to be familiar, with the contents of these reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also say that you provided elements used to compile the reports. Can you tell us which -- what kind of information you provided on the basis of which such reports were compiled? Could you provide us with an example.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: I said I did participate to a certain extent. I provided certain information on the enemy, above all. And that was my main task in general. Information on the enemy, the enemy's purposes, targets, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, do you recognise this kind of report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a regular combat report for the 25th of June, 1993, at 1700 hours?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, that can be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under item 1 of this report, does it say, under item 1, enemy during the day, the enemy violated cease-fire agreements in the following manner --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I'm afraid I am a bit lost. When you were talking about reports, Ms. Pilipovic referred to duty officers' reports on the situation with regard to 12-hour periods to the command at these morning meetings. Did I understand you correctly that this was reports to the commander of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, when you were asked to a provide a basis for the knowledge of the witness, you asked him about reports and whether he was familiar with it, et cetera, et cetera. I understood this to me, and this was confirmed now by the witness, to be reports to the commander of the SRK. What you are showing us now seems to be a report by the command of the SRK to the headquarters of the VRS, which is as far as my knowledge goes is a different type of report. So I'm a bit confused as to laying the basis for the knowledge of the witness by reports to the SRK command where you confront us now, as far as I can see, with a report which at least reads that it's signed by the commander to the VRS staff. So I'm -- perhaps you could solve my problem of understanding the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. The first report that the witness recognised was a report from the command of the Light Infantry Brigade Rajlovac which was forwarded to the command of the SRK. The second report which the witness has also recognised is a report which was forwarded to the VRS main staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, can you tell us whether the regular combat reports which were compiled in the command of the SRK were reported to the main staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes. As I have just said, I just explained how it was possible for me to be familiar with the contents of such reports. I provided certain elements from my own field or my department's fields. And because of this, I was in a position to be familiar with the contents of such reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The report that you have in front of you, D719 dated the 25th of June, 1993, does this report contain a summary of all the information that the duty officer received in the corps command? So from all subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This is a collection of reports from subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it says in reports of this kind that the enemy violated cease-fire agreements, does this explain that the violations took place in the SRK zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does item 1, therefore, state which positions are concerned? Does it state where the cease-fire agreement was violated, at which positions it was violated?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it says that action was taken in the Dobrinja area, in the Pretis area, the Rajlovac Light Infantry Brigade, the Sokolj reservoir, the Nedzarici settlement, and the infantry weapons and rifle-launched grenades and occasionally 82 mortars were used to shell these areas, do the contents of item 1 summarise the reports made in the course of the day from all the subordinate units with regard to the area where the cease-fire agreement was violated?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If in the course of that day or during that period, a cease-fire was in force, a cease-fire that had been signed was in force, does this report state that there was fighting, that there was shooting in the corps's zone of responsibility in the course of that day?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. We characterise such action as provocative action on the part of the enemy. And usually, this action wasn't responded to, and the commanders of the subordinate units emphasised this fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that there was no response to this action. Can you tell us why there was no response to such action on the part of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Well, we considered this kind of action to be provocative, as I have already said. And on numerous occasions, it was possible to see that they wanted to provoke a reaction on our part. And they would then take advantage of this in the media, and as a rule, the Serbian side would be accused of having violated the cease-fire. Since we were aware of these propaganda tricks that the enemy used, I know that the commander insisted and encouraged his subordinate commanders not to fall for such tricks. And the subordinate commanders respected these instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, looking at the clock, I would think that it would be time --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we can have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes. Ms. Pilipovic, if my bookkeeping is correct, you spent a little bit over two and a half hours in examination-in-chief until now, and I think you scheduled four hours for it. Yes, we'll adjourn until 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is it you who is going to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have the impression that there will be a change with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in order to save time -- I would like to say thank you, first of all. In order to save time -- I would like to say good day first of all. But I'm going to show you some documents, and I would appreciate it if you could examine each document and to tell us whether you recognise the documents, and whether as far as the contents are concerned the dates are correct and whether there was a large-scale fighting such as it is described. Have you understood this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, we will use several documents at the same time. There are several of them. I will give you a list. Could you please distribute them. The dates we are interested in concern some of the incidents mentioned in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that your question to the witness is whether he can confirm the combat activities as described in the documents in the -- at the locations described in the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you have a look at the documents while we are waiting, please. Please take a look at the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Usher, I think it is not necessary to have all the documents put on the ELMO, please. It is not necessary. [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know if the registrar has the -- had the time to distribute all the documents, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have received three now. And perhaps you start with any of these three and I take it that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I wanted to move on more rapidly, but we'll manage like this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, take any one of the documents and please give me the date.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The document dated the 13th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The document in question is Document Number 1144. First of all, do you recognise this document? Do you recognise the date and the fighting that is mentioned in the document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: As I said, this is a regular combat report from the corps command. It went to the main staff of the VRS army. It's a standard type of document. It mentions the action that enemy took towards Ilidza, Hadzici, Rajlovac, Grbavica, et cetera. Given that it's written on the basis of reports from subordinate commanders, the contents under item 1 are true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please take a second document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, may I ask for a clarification of the witness. How do I have to understand your answer, that you say, "well, it is the usual type of document which was drafted on the basis of reports, and therefore I take it that the contents will reflect reality," or are you telling us I have a personal, specific remembrance of what happened on the 13th of November, and therefore I can confirm on the basis of that that the information contained in this document is a true reflection of what happened on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember one event in particular on the basis of which I can link this to the other events. This has to do with a Browning opening fire from Muslim positions, firing on Mojmilo at the Lukavica crossroads. I know that on that occasion, a woman was wounded at the crossroads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, when you answer the questions, indicate as you did it now, that you say there is a specific point on which I have personal recollection of this element of the report, that it took place. I know that from my personal experience. Would you please always indicate that, and that would then distinguish the confirmation in more general terms. You say: "This is the type of report, and I know how they were drafted, and therefore I take them to reflect the events, although I did not have any specific personal recollection or -- in mind." Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. With your permission, I would like to ask for a necessary clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in response to a question from the Chamber, you said that a woman was wounded it appears at the crossroads. My question is as follows: Was this woman a member of the army corps, or was she a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, no. She was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Why was she wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The crossroads mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question "why she was wounded" is really asking the witness to speculate about things which he would not know about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please -- well, you couldn't say that. Usually Defence have many causes. I take it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that you are interested to know one or more of these causes. Would you please specify in such a way. And I take it -- unless you have specific reasons to ask about the intent of those who might have caused the injury. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, with regard to this incident, this civilian woman who was wounded and whom you yourself have mentioned, can you tell us what happened, in what circumstances it happened, was she accompanied by soldiers, was she on her own, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Well, the crossroads -- this happened at the crossroads. And as far as I can remember, it was at about 1.00 in the afternoon. The witness I spoke to, and I remember this, claimed that the woman was walking on her own at the crossroads. She was alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was she involved in some sort of event, some sort of military event, although she was alone? She could have found herself in the midst of an exchange of fire, et cetera, et cetera. What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, it was a fairly peaceful day. And the fire opened from the enemy Browning, from this position, was not something that was customary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you have confirmed this. I would now like you to take another document, and could you give us the date of the document, please. Which document do you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The document is dated the 12th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question is the same: Again, do you recognise this type of document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And as far as the description of the fighting is concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a document 12th of March, 1994. Is that the document you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's Document Number 542.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what can you tell us about the fighting that was ongoing at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Here they mention enemy action, which was customary. And there is nothing here that I could confirm, that I could fully confirm, nothing under item 1 of this document. But the -- this kind of action happened so frequently that it's almost impossible to remember something concrete and to confirm what has been mentioned under item 1, what has been alleged under item 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, you mentioned frequent occurrences. You mentioned something that happened very often with regard to item 1. Would you also include sniper activity that is mentioned there? I'm speaking about the frequency.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you please take the third document, put this on the side. Can you tell us the date so that we can find it. Please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The date of this document is 9th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So I'm asking you the same question again.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, it says here that the enemy was involved in provocation, and this is precisely what I told you a moment ago. And the sectors that the enemy was firing from, these are very well known to me. And it is true that the enemy fired from infantry or artillery weapons very frequently from there. There was sniper fire on Vrace, Dobrinja, Grbavica, and Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just rise to indicate to remind counsel and the Court whether the witness could indicate whether he speaks of these things from his knowledge or he is just regurgitating what he reads in the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I understand the answer of the witness, unless he specifically points at personal experience, he is merely reproducing the text and perhaps gives his comments on whether this was -- these were usual events or whether it would surprise him, this to have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what I wish to say is that there is a sentence that was translated into English. In any case, the second -- "known to me." These are very well known to me. This is what the witness said: "These are very well known to me" So he is speaking about these areas in time of war. We are not asking him whether today whether these areas are different. So I believe that this is how he expressed his personal position, as to what he recalls. But I can of course ask the question again in a different way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please, when you tell us what you just told us, is this a personal knowledge that you have of this, or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Here I think I can link it to a memory. I believe that the date is linked to one of the attempts to cut off communication, that is the road between Lukavica and Pale. It is one of the unsuccessful attempts by the Muslim side that took place in the area of Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the transcript, the previous document -- the previous document was 542. And the current document, this is 1631.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please take another document and we can do the same exercise again. Tell us the date, and then tell us if you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The date is 17th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the record, this is Document 588.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the contents?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: I cannot specifically recall the events because after all, this was ten years ago. But I believe that they reflect what really happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the level of the information, the influx of information which was internal, is there any imaginable situation whereby a false information would be given? Could this have occurred? In this document, could it have been something that was falsely given?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: As far as reporting of the subordinate is concerned -- of the superior is concerned, the duty of the subordinate is to enter into the report well-checked details, authentic information. Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please take another document. Can you tell us the date, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: 11th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the transcript, document is D825.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the same exercise, sir, please. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Item 1, in relation to provocation or attacks of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Considering the date, I remember that in July, I stayed for about five days on this part of the front. I remember that there was an intense infantry attack by the enemy on some parts of the Zuc elevation. And that was in the area of responsibility of the Vogosca Brigade. And I remember that there were casualties, there were people who were killed. I don't remember their names, but I remember that we had casualties. I am certain that this is precisely this that was mentioned in this report, 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, you tell us about the casualties that you suffered. In fact, you even said "on our side." That is the reason why I'm asking you the question. Do you mean on your side in terms of military side, or do you mean civilian victims -- and civilian victims or just civilian victims?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Considering this event, these were troops, these were soldiers, because combat operations occurred outside the open area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the same period that we are looking at, do you know if bearing in mind this offensive, there were also reactions, tensions, exchanges of fire in other areas? And I am asking this in relation to Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Considering that I was in the area of responsibility of the Vogosca Brigade, and considering that I know about this event, I presume that the other information included in item -- in this item are also correct. But I was not in a position to see this for myself considering that I was in a completely other area of the area of responsibility of the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, can you please take another document and tell us the date.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Document dated 24th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I have the same question again in relation to this form.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, the form is recognisable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the date? Does it remind you of anything?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, it reminds me, this being the date of the Lukavac Operation, Lukavac 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will come back to that very briefly. Mr. President, for the transcript, this is D837 exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to item 1, the enemy actions, et cetera, what can you tell us about this, the provocation and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: So this is Operation Lukavac 1993. At approximately this period of time, I was myself in the area of Mount Igman where, in the area of Malo Polje located on Mount Igman, we had fierce clashes with enemy forces, enemy forces coming from the direction of Tresnjevo Brdo and Brezovaca. So this is the event I recall. Also the other activities, that is, operations that are listed here, did take place because the enemy from the part of town under Muslim control operated, fired, on a daily basis, predominantly with snipers -- or from snipers in order to get the pressure off their forces at Mount Igman which were retreating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, considering we are not speaking the same language, you can go a bit faster with your answers. Thank you very much. You're talking about combat activities. I can see that there is a sniper activity which provoked a civilian. Can you tell us something about that that you recall.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, I don't. No, I don't recall that. I don't recall that, but the civilian is a victim, is a casualty here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. If you don't recall, that's very well. You told us that these were authentic documents in their contents. Therefore, when there was firing in the direction of Grbavica, did you know, you, who were in charge of intelligence services, what were the areas that sniper fire was coming from, from the other side?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: It was very hard to identify these places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Because a sniper who is a marksman is first of all well camouflaged. He is well hidden. He also has a special weapon, specialist weapon, mostly it is a rifle with a silencer. And most of the time, he would only fire once from one position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know if the enemy party had -- the enemy side had such equipment in order to facilitate this -- technical equipment to facilitate this for their troops? Do they have, for instance, optical sights, optical equipment to do this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: It's difficult to give a brief answer to this question, but I will do my best. So first of all, the enemy certainly had at their disposal quite a high quality equipment, sniping equipment, that is, rifle and optical sight. Moreover, we shouldn't forget that it was under their control that the factory, Zrak, was, and this is the factory that produced such optical devices. So the fact itself that there was a special unit in charge only of sniping, they were called "Seve," this says enough about the importance and the attention that was had and given by the Muslim army to that part of their activities. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm going to come back to another one of your answers. You said that it was very hard for several reasons to determine the place, that there was camouflaging of the position, that they would also use a silencer when sniping, and also that they would be changing places. So you're saying that the sniper, if I understood you correctly, would only use one location once. Is that correct? Did I understand you correctly? I believe in the transcript, that's what you were saying, that a sniper would fire from one position once, and would then change position. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: In some literature which deals with these matters, among other things, I read that this was the golden rule of sniping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm going to stop you here. Why was that? What was the reason? Why is this a golden rule?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Well, I can just elaborate briefly in my answer. This happened in the battle of the old town. Because of sniping activity, the rule is applied today. Because a real sniper, a professional, would only fire once. And the reason for that would be that the sniper wouldn't be spotted, and then killed himself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter correction: The battle of Stalingrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you're telling us about Stalingrad. This takes us back somewhat. But what you're telling us of Stalingrad, is this something that can be applied in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Well, this parallel couldn't be applied fully, couldn't be drawn fully, but there are many elements that could be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, what would be the consequence if a sniper found a spot, a location, which was perfectly convenient for his activity, for the shooting, and if he then proceeded to make this his own nest, referring to what -- the term we use? Now, in military technique, if a sniper shoots systematically from the same location, and I'm talking about the reaction from the opposing side, what would happen then?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: If such a --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At this point, I have tried not to rise. But the witness had indicated already that he's speaking from literature that he has read and he went on to indicate that he's drawing analogies from Stalingrad. We are now exploring his personal knowledge of sniping or are we exploring his knowledge of literature or history in respect to sniping? Perhaps that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, here we are dealing with an officer with a lot of experience who, contrary to all of us, has lived through the events of Sarajevo. And unfortunately not like all of us, he's read about what's happened in Stalingrad. And he certainly has first hand experience --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you please, if you ask the witness about it, ask with such precision that we know what he's talking about. So the question was about what one could expect the opposing party to do if a sniper nest would be established. So there are two questions. First is what in theory you would have to do; and the second question would be what you experienced that was ever done in such a situation. And then please describe that situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If enemy activity of a sniper would be spotted, then the troops on the first line would on their own initiative if they spotted him, they would then fire. They would shoot in his direction in order to eliminate the target, eliminate the enemy target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please listen carefully to the question. The question is about what is called a sniper's nest. And Mr. Piletta-Zanin explained what it is, that is a position where a sniper felt such at ease that he would repeatedly fire from that position. What would a military response be, I take it at least you want a military response, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, to such an established sniper nest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I was clear. If such a target would be seen, observed, then it would be -- attempts would be made to neutralise it with adequate fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely. You're speaking of neutralisation with adequate fire. Can you please give us a little more detail.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: If I commanded a unit which was targeted by sniper fire, and if I observed such a sniper, then I would try and have him neutralised with adequate means as soon as possible. If we look at the features of the location where the sniper is firing from, then I would use a tank fire because I would want to make sure that he was neutralised, that this nest was neutralised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would the same result be accomplished by a lighter weapon? For instance, using something like smaller calibre weapon, say 20 millimetre, or a heavy machine-gun, or some, say, weapons using incendiary ammunition? Could the same be accomplished with those? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Possible, possible, possible to have that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. To that extent, do you know if Sarajevo forces had at their disposal weapons that could possibly destroy such sniper facilities if there were any?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: We did. Sarajevo Romanija Corps had such weapons to neutralise any terrorist targets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the other side. Do you know if the Muslim side had such weapons which would allow them to destroy, and this is a theoretical question, to allow them to destroy possible sniper positions if there were any?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you are talking about if there were any sniper positions on our side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. They had such weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, could you please take other documents and carry out the same exercise with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, in the beginning you explained that we had the theoretical knowledge of the witness and the practical experience of the witness. So the next question I suggested be put to him, whether he had any experience either that your forces would respond to sniping fire from the opposite side, or that the opposite side, and not limiting it to the Sarajevo area in the time we are discussing here, but whether you ever were in a position where the forces you were in would respond to sniper fire from the other side, or whether you ever experienced that an opposing party would respond to sniping fire from the force you were serving in, whether you have any practical experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No particular practical experience, apart from the fact that I was personally targeted by a sniper on three occasions. Fortunately, the sniper missed on each occasion. When fire is opened in such situations, this is usually because of requests from men at the front lines because if sniper activity can be observed, these are the men who are in the best position to observe from which position sniper fire is being opened. But I can't remember any particular situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please take another document and tell us the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I do not -- I had in one of your answers on this document, that's the reason why I'm asking now because otherwise we have to find that document, I remember that date because it was the operation Lukavac 1993. Could you just very briefly explain what you understood to be Operation Lukavac 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's one of the questions I was going to put later on, but we can do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was in relation for this document that the witness told us. But if you're dealing with it at a later stage, that's fine --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, time is the main problem. I'm trying to go fast but I think we will need a little time tomorrow, too, since matters are not easy as we might think. Let the witness respond to the question about the operation Lukavac 1993, and then we shall carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the document of the 24th of July, 1993, which mentions these events, these events are familiar to me because the operation Lukavac 1993 was ongoing at the time. I don't know what interests you with regard to this operation. Could you be so kind as to rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you briefly explain what the operation was about. Because you mention it without explaining what it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try and be brief. I think that you know part of the response to this question. The operation Lukavac 1993 is an operation which was carried out in the wider area of the zone of responsibility of the SRK. And it was led by the main staff of the VRS, of the Republika Srpska army. Units from the entire area of Republika Srpska participated in this operation. The operation was carried out in order to improve the operative positions of the corps. And it came to an end because of pressure from the international forces and because of the Security Council decision, the UN Security Council decision. I think that was on the 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Could you take another document, please. And give us the date. And do you recognise this type of document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes. The date of the document is the 5th of August, 1993. And I do recognise this type of document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you have a look at the contents, at what it says about military action which is under item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And during -- while we're waiting, this document is D935.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: I recognise the events in this document. That is to say, the action taken against the 1st Sarajevo Motorised Brigade. I think that this was the first time the enemy used a 30 through 2 gun through the Mojmilo hill. I apologise, a 20 through 3. That means a 20 millimetre gun with 3 barrels. So this type of field gun hadn't been used until then from the Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd be grateful if you could focus on an aspect which I am interested in. It's the very first point, it's the very first paragraph. It's the first line where the cease-fire violation is mentioned. In the course of your testimony, you said that the enemy side always violated these agreements. I would first of all like you to tell us why and on what basis you can make such a claim. And then perhaps give us one or two examples. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, the witness is asked why he can make such a claim. We have no foundation for this as to whether or not the claim or the statement made in this document is the witness document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're asking why, Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Isn't Mr. Piletta-Zanin asking for the basis of the claim? The claim is violations took place. It says why and on what basis you can make such a claim? Isn't that an invitation to express himself why he can tell us, on the basis of what, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is not my interpretation of the question. The question asks the witness to explain why he makes such a claim. If one could make a claim like that, it would be different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how I understood the question. Let's hear the answer from the witness, and then we'll see whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think in French the question was very clear, if we were to pay attention to being perfect with our languages, we should pay attention to the text. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, nobody is perfect, not even the Bench. Could you please answer the question, that the enemy side always violated these cease-fire agreements. Could you explain to us on the basis of on what you could draw this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is quite simple: On the basis of my personal experience and on the basis of the personal information I had. And secondly, I would like to say that the Serbian side was always in favour of truces. It was always in favour of peace, and there are several reasons for this, one of the main ones being was that the SRK were fairly tired from all the fighting and we quite simply didn't have the force to respond to enemy provocations or attacks. In any event, truces were suitable for us. We were in favour of truces. And we respected each truce.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is my question last question, and then we will conclude for this afternoon. Witness, this document refers to the Kobilja Glava area which we can see at the end of item 1. Do you remember military activity of any kind which may have happened in this area which is called Kobilja Glava?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: I can't remember this specific event.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, I think it's time to adjourn and with your permission, we'll continue with our examination of this witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I notice that there's approximately half an hour left. Would you please keep that in mind when continuing your examination-in-chief tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll try to do so, Mr. President. There have been a few interruptions which did not seem to be absolutely necessary to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The level of interpretation has not been such -- of such extraordinary nature that it would justify to depart from the time claimed. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the same courtroom. And may I instruct you, Mr. Witness, not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given in this Court and the testimony you're still about to give in this Court. We'll adjourn until 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 1.46 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 28th day of January, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
